```{r setup, include = FALSE}
has_igraph <- requireNamespace("igraph", quietly = TRUE)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.width = 6.5,
  fig.height = 4,
  dpi = 100
)
library(citelens)
```

## Introduction

The [Getting started](citelens.html) vignette covers getting records into R:
converting RefWorks and RIS exports, reading BibTeX, parsing Google Scholar
results, and filling in missing abstracts. This vignette covers what you can do
once you have a data frame of papers. Four tools are described here:

| Question | Function |
|---|---|
| Is the same paper listed twice? | `find_duplicate_papers()`, `dedupe_papers()` |
| Which papers, venues and authors are cited most? | `citation_rank()` |
| Who writes together, and in which groups? | `author_network()` and its plots |
| How does the vocabulary of abstracts change over time? | `abstract_ca()` |

None of them needs a Scopus or Web of Science subscription. They work on the
data frames that the rest of citelens produces, or on any data frame with the
right columns.

The network plots use the igraph package, which is not required by the rest of
citelens. Install it with `install.packages("igraph")` if you want them.

## Sample data

The examples use two small data sets that ship with the package. Both are
synthetic: the names, titles and abstracts are invented.

```{r sample-data}
f <- system.file("extdata", "sample_authors.csv", package = "citelens")
papers <- read.csv(f, stringsAsFactors = FALSE)
dim(papers)
head(papers, 4)
```

`sample_authors.csv` has 18 rows with the columns the functions expect by
default: `title`, `authors` (separated by " and "), `year` and `cited_by`. If
your data comes from `bib_to_df()` the author column is called `author`, and
the functions below detect it automatically. If your columns have other names,
every function has arguments (`title`, `authors`, `year`, `cites`) to say which
column is which.

## Finding duplicate papers

Google Scholar and reference managers often list one paper more than once: a
journal version and a preprint, a re-indexed copy with a single citation, a
reprint with a new year. Left alone, duplicates inflate citation counts and make
two authors look as if they wrote more papers together than they did.
`find_duplicate_papers()` flags likely duplicates without changing your data.

```{r duplicates}
dups <- find_duplicate_papers(papers)
dups
```

Rows 1 and 7 are the same paper: the title differs only by a full stop, the
year differs, and the second copy has one citation. The most-cited copy in each
group is marked `KEEP`.

Titles are compared after lower-casing and removing accents, punctuation and
extra spaces. By default (`method = "near"`) titles that are within 8% of each
other by edit distance also match, which catches a missing word or a typo. Use
`method = "exact"` to require identical normalised titles, or change the
tolerance with `max_dist`.

### Same title, different paper

Generic titles are common. Row 18 of the sample data has exactly the same title
as row 1, but it is by different authors and is a different paper. It is not
flagged, because by default a pair must also share at least one author surname
(`require_author_overlap = TRUE`). Turning the check off shows what would
happen otherwise:

```{r overlap}
find_duplicate_papers(papers, require_author_overlap = FALSE)
```

Keep the default unless your data has no author information.

### Removing duplicates

Review the list first, then let `dedupe_papers()` drop the less-cited copies:

```{r dedupe}
clean <- dedupe_papers(papers)
nrow(clean)
attr(clean, "dropped")
```

If you disagree with the automatic choice, name the rows to drop yourself with
`drop_rows = c(7)`.

You rarely need to call these functions directly. `author_network()` and
`citation_rank()` both remove duplicate listings by default and tell you which
rows they dropped. Use `dedupe = FALSE` in either to count every row.

## Ranking by citations

`citation_rank()` ranks papers, venues or authors by citation count and
computes citation indices for the whole collection.

```{r rank}
res <- citation_rank(papers, current_year = 2024)
res
```

The message says that the duplicate listing was removed before counting. The
top block shows the indices for the collection:

* **h-index**: the largest *h* such that *h* papers each have at least *h*
  citations.
* **g-index**: the largest *g* such that the top *g* papers together have at
  least *g*^2^ citations (capped at the number of papers).
* **i10-index**: the number of papers with at least 10 citations.

The table has one row per paper. Besides `citations` it has a `percentile`
(the percent of papers with strictly fewer citations), the share of all
citations, a running total (`cum_share`), the paper's age, and
`cites_per_year`, which is useful for comparing an older paper with a recent
one. The examples pass `current_year = 2024` so the output does not change as
the calendar does; by default the current year is used.

Ties share a rank, and the next rank is skipped (for example 1, 1, 3).

### Authors and venues

Use `by` to rank something other than papers. For authors, each author is
credited with the full citation count of every paper they appear on:

```{r rank-author}
citation_rank(papers, by = "author", top_n = 6)$ranked
```

Each author gets their own `h_index`, computed from their papers. Ranking
venues needs a `venue` column, as produced by `scholar_parse_html()` and
`bib_to_df()`: `citation_rank(d, by = "venue")`.

`top_n` shortens the table but never the indices, which are always computed on
the full data. The result is a list, so `res$index` and `res$ranked` are plain
data frames you can write to Excel or plot.

## Co-authorship networks

`author_network()` turns the author lists into a network. Authors are the
nodes. Two authors are joined by a line if they share a paper, and the line's
weight is the number of papers they share.

```{r network, eval = has_igraph}
net <- author_network(papers)
net
```

The message shows that duplicates were removed first. Without that step, the
duplicate copy of row 1 would make its authors look like they had written one
more paper together than they did.

The printed summary describes the whole network: the number of authors and
connections, how many separate groups there are, the share of authors in the
largest group, and the modularity of the communities that Louvain clustering
found. The table underneath lists authors by *strength*, the sum of their edge
weights.

### What is inside

```{r network-parts, eval = has_igraph}
names(net)
net$components
```

* `nodes` has one row per author: papers, total citations, degree (number of
  distinct co-authors), strength, betweenness, closeness, eigenvector
  centrality, and the component and community each author belongs to.
* `edges` lists the author pairs and their weights.
* `summary` has the network-level statistics.
* `communities` summarises each Louvain community.
* `components` has one row per connected group of authors: who is in it, how
  many papers produced it, its total citations and its most-cited paper. The
  `component` number is the ID used on the plots and in the functions below.
* `duplicates` holds any rows that were dropped as duplicates.

A collection of unrelated papers produces many small disconnected groups,
because every paper's author list is a clique. Betweenness is non-zero only for
authors who connect others *within* a group, and when most groups are separate,
communities simply coincide with components. Read these statistics with that in
mind.

### Drawing the groups

`plot()` draws one small map for each group of authors who published together:

```{r network-plot, eval = has_igraph, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 6}
plot(net)
```

Each dot is an author. An orange line, with a number on it, joins two authors
who published together more than once, and the number is how many papers. A
gray line joins two authors who shared one paper. Each panel is named after the
strongest pair in the group. Groups from a single paper are left out by
default, and when more groups qualify than fit on the page, the ones with the
most papers are drawn. Control this with `min_papers`, `max_panels` and
`components`.

For a single combined picture, use `type = "overview"`. Dots are coloured by
the total citations of the author's papers and sized by collaboration strength,
and the `#` labels match the IDs in `net$components`:

```{r network-overview, eval = has_igraph, fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4.5}
plot(net, type = "overview", label_top = 8)
```

### One cluster at a time

`plot_cluster()` draws a single group, which is useful for slides. Use the
component ID from `net$components`:

```{r network-cluster, eval = has_igraph, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 4}
plot_cluster(net, net$components$component[1])
```

The layout is arranged by an algorithm and only the connections carry meaning,
so rerunning with a different `seed` gives a different but equivalent
arrangement. For a general audience try `core_only = TRUE`, which shows only
authors on two or more papers, and `simple = TRUE`, which makes the dots and
labels larger.

### Filtering to repeat collaborators

Many collections contain mostly one-off groups. `min_component_papers` drops
every group supported by fewer than that many papers before any statistics are
computed, so the metrics, communities and IDs all describe the filtered
network:

```{r network-filter, eval = has_igraph}
net2 <- author_network(papers, min_component_papers = 2)
net2$components[, c("component", "n_authors", "n_papers", "top_paper")]
```

### Saving maps

`cluster_maps()` writes a map for every group, either as one PNG per group, one
multi-page PDF, or both. It never writes anything unless you give it a
location:

```{r cluster-maps, eval = FALSE}
cluster_maps(net2, dir = "cluster_maps", pdf = "cluster_maps.pdf")
```

If your system has no working PNG device (a headless server without X11, for
example) the PNG files are skipped with a warning, and the PDF is still
written.

### Caveats about the data

Google Scholar shortens long author lists with "...". The authors at the end of
a long list are missing from `scholar_parse_html()` results, so collaborations
that involve them are not seen. Also, a citation count belongs to the paper and
not to any one author, so `total_citations` gives each author full credit for
every paper they appear on.

## Correspondence analysis of abstracts

`abstract_ca()` asks how the vocabulary of a set of abstracts differs between
groups of papers, using correspondence analysis. Here the groups are time
periods. It builds a table of word counts by period, then finds the few
dimensions that best separate the periods and the words that drive the
separation.

The sample abstracts are synthetic, so they contain some filler words that would
dominate the result. In real data you would use your own stop-word list, if
any:

```{r ca}
f <- system.file("extdata", "sample_abstracts.bib", package = "citelens")
refs <- bib_to_df(f)
filler <- c("note", "time", "follow", "shape", "touch", "studied",
            "evidence", "work", "attention", "discussion")

ca <- abstract_ca(refs, breaks = c(2017, 2020), stopwords = filler,
                  min_doc_freq = 3)
ca
```

The periods come from `breaks`, which here means before 2017, 2017 to 2019 and
2020 onward. Leave `breaks` out and the function creates `n_periods`
equal-sized periods instead. The inertia table shows how much of the
differences each dimension captures. The final block lists, for each period, the
words used much more than average, ranked by *lift* (how many times more
frequent a word is in that period than in the whole collection).

```{r ca-distinctive}
head(ca$distinctive, 6)
```

The plot puts periods and words on the same two dimensions. Periods that sit
close together used similar vocabulary, and a word near a period is
characteristic of it:

```{r ca-plot, fig.width = 6.5, fig.height = 5}
plot(ca)
```

Some practical points:

* Only abstracts with at least `min_words` words (default 30) and a valid year
  are used, and only words in at least `min_doc_freq` abstracts (default 5)
  enter the analysis. Lower these for small collections, and raise them for
  large ones to keep the plot readable.
* `min_count` sets how many times a word must be used within a period before it
  can be listed as distinctive for that period.
* The function needs a reasonable number of abstracts; it stops with a message
  if there are fewer than 20 usable ones.
* Correspondence analysis describes association, not cause. A word that is
  distinctive of a period tells you what authors wrote about then, not why.

## Putting it together

A typical session with a Google Scholar export looks like this:

```{r workflow, eval = FALSE}
d <- scholar_parse_html("scholar_results.html")

find_duplicate_papers(d)            # review before anything is dropped
rank <- citation_rank(d)            # indices and top papers
rank_au <- citation_rank(d, by = "author", top_n = 20)

net <- author_network(d, min_component_papers = 2)
plot(net)
cluster_maps(net, pdf = "cluster_maps.pdf")

ca <- abstract_ca(d, text = "abstract")   # when you have abstracts
plot(ca)
```

Results are plain lists of data frames, so you can write any table to Excel with
`writexl::write_xlsx()` or continue the analysis in your own code. If your
records are missing abstracts, the OpenAlex lookup described in the
[Getting started](citelens.html) vignette can fill many of them in.

## Good to know

* Everything runs locally. Nothing is sent anywhere, except the explicit
  OpenAlex lookup in the other vignette.
* Citation counts are only as good as their source. A Scholar count is not a
  Scopus or Web of Science count, so compare indices only within one source.
* Duplicate detection is a heuristic. Review `find_duplicate_papers()` when the
  decision matters, and use `dedupe = FALSE` or `drop_rows` to override it.
* Please report problems or ideas at
  <https://github.com/cownr10r/citelens/issues>.
